opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam, it's great to be here.

It's been a pretty natural evolution, honestly. I started out squarely in computer vision, working on things like attributes and how we describe visual content. Very early on, I found myself drawn to the question of how humans actually interact with these systems. When you think about attributes, you're already thinking about language, because attributes are the words people use to describe what they see. So language crept in almost from the start.

From there, I became really interested in problems where vision and language had to work together. Visual Question Answering was a big one for us. The idea was that if a system can answer arbitrary, open-ended questions about an image, that's a much richer test of understanding than just labeling objects. That led to visual dialog, where the system has to hold a conversation about an image and keep track of context across turns, and then to embodied settings, where an agent has to navigate or act in an environment based on natural language instructions.

What ties all of it together for me is that I care about AI systems that are useful to people and that people can communicate with naturally. Humans don't experience the world one modality at a time. We see, we talk, we hear, and we act, all at once. So if you want AI that can collaborate with us, it has to bridge those modalities.

More recently, that's pulled me toward generative and creative work, things like generating images and video from text. There's something exciting about systems that don't just understand content but help people create it, whether that's an artist exploring ideas or someone without technical skills expressing something they imagine. So the thread through all of it has been less about any single modality and more about building AI that connects to how people think, communicate, and create.

r001.rationale: The response says her interest in how people interact with AI led from attributes and language into problems where vision and language work together, and ties that work to natural communication with AI.

r002.rationale: It says her interest shifted toward generative and creative work because these systems can help people create and express what they imagine.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I never really thought of vision as the end goal. For me, vision was always a way into the bigger question of how you build machines that can perceive the world and then actually communicate with people about it. Early on, a lot of my work was on things like attributes, so describing objects in terms of properties rather than just category labels. And once you start caring about descriptions, you're already halfway to language, because the natural interface for a human to tell a machine what they mean, or to correct it, is language.

That led pretty directly to visual question answering, where you show the system an image and ask it a free-form question in natural language. VQA was interesting because it forced the model to actually ground language in the pixels, and it also exposed how much these systems were leaning on language priors instead of looking. You could answer "what color is the banana" with "yellow" and never look at the image. So a lot of my research became about that interplay, about making the vision and the language genuinely talk to each other rather than one modality quietly doing all the work.

From there it felt natural to keep widening the aperture. We did work on visual dialog, where it's not a single question but a conversation about an image, so now you have to maintain context over turns. We looked at embodied settings, where an agent has to navigate a space and answer questions, so perception, language, and action all have to come together. And more recently I've been drawn to generative work, to creativity, to systems that can produce images, audio, video, and respond to what a person wants to make. That's been personally meaningful because I have an art practice myself, and I'm curious about tools that extend human creativity rather than replace it.

So I'd say the through line is that the interesting problems live at the boundaries between modalities, and between the model and the person using it. Vision on its own is a bit like studying one sense in isolation. The richer questions show up when you ask how all of it fits together.

r001.rationale: She says she wanted machines to perceive the world and communicate with people, and that this led from vision to language-grounded VQA and other vision-language work.

r002.rationale: She links her own art practice and interest in extending human creativity to her recent interest in generative systems.

astra-6.text:
My research has largely been motivated by understanding how we can build AI systems that have some of the capabilities we take for granted in humans. Computer vision is a natural starting point because so much of how we understand the world comes from what we see. But vision doesn’t operate in isolation. We use language to describe what we see, to ask questions, and to communicate our understanding to someone else.

That led me toward problems at the intersection of vision and language, such as visual question answering. Given an image and a question about it, can a system provide an answer? What I find interesting is that the question can demand very different kinds of understanding—recognizing an object, understanding a relationship, or reasoning about what might be happening.

And that opens up a broader interest in human-AI interaction. If we want systems that people can work with naturally, those systems need to connect what they perceive with what people say and mean. So, for me, moving into multimodal AI is a continuation of that underlying motivation.

r001.rationale: The response says that building systems people can work with naturally led from computer vision to vision-and-language problems and multimodal AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention creative expression or generative models.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the underlying interest is in how we build AI systems that understand the world and can communicate with people about it. Computer vision gives us one piece of that: understanding what’s in an image. But when you start asking what someone might want to know about that image, language becomes a natural part of the problem.

Think about answering a question about an image. The system needs to understand the question, identify the relevant visual information, and connect the two. That pushes us beyond recognizing objects toward reasoning about relationships and context.

So I see multimodal AI as a natural extension of computer vision. The broader goal is to bring perception and language together so that people can interact with these systems in more useful, intuitive ways.

r001.rationale: The response connects her broader goal of making AI interaction more useful and intuitive with bringing perception and language together, presenting multimodal AI as a natural extension of computer vision.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention creative expression or generative models.
